headline: Senate passes college sports bill, 77-22. The House is out.
summary: The Protect College Sports Act cleared the Senate on Monday, 77 to 22. It lets the NCAA set and enforce one national rulebook on transfers, recruiting and paying players. A school can share about $50 million a year with athletes, who get five years of eligibility and one free transfer. The House left for the election on September 16.
cover_answer: So every school plays by one rulebook.
table_question: Who should write the rules of a game: the players or the league?

5-7.script: The people who make our country's laws voted last night on rules for college sports, the games on TV on Saturdays. The rules say how players can switch teams and how much a college can pay them. It's like every school agreeing on one rulebook before kickoff instead of each bringing its own. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: The Saturday game they already know, and one rulebook for it.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and "name, image and likeness" is in front of nobody. The script gives them the Saturday game on TV and one shared rulebook, the thing they already argue about at recess. Expect "do the players get money?" Yes, some do, and the new rules say how much a school can pay.

8-12.script: College players can now earn money and switch schools through a transfer portal. The Senate voted 77 to 22 for one national rulebook: the NCAA enforces it, players get five years and one free transfer. One referee, one rulebook. The House has to vote too, and it went home for the election.
8-12.why: A chain, a referee, then a House that went home.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether adults apply them evenly, so the script hands them the chain: players earning money, a vote, one rulebook, a referee to enforce it. The catch is the point: the House has to vote too, and it left town. Expect "so is it a law?" Not yet. Cruz wants the House back for a day.

13-17.script: Should Congress write the rules for a game? The Senate just did, 77 to 22: one national rulebook, a cap on player pay, one free transfer. Second: Ted Cruz wants the House back for a day so Trump can sign it on the College GameDay set before the election. Governing, or campaigning?
13-17.why: The rulebook question, then the campaign question.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the bill can be a real fix for college sports and a signing on the College GameDay set can be an election ad. The script gives them both and lets them argue which. Expect "why is Cruz so keen?" He told Semafor that voters who ignore politics care deeply about college sports.

5-7.a: Yes, some do now. The new rules say how much a school can pay, about $50 million a year to share.

8-12.a: How a college player switches schools. The bill allows one free transfer.
No. The House has to vote too, and it went home on September 16.

13-17.a: One national rulebook on pay, transfers and conferences, with the NCAA enforcing it.

13-17.q: Does Trump have to sign it?
13-17.a: Yes, once the House passes it. Cruz wants a College GameDay signing.
